description: We’re building something new for the Red Planet. It’s a way to see Mars the way no explorer has before: where to go, what lies beneath, and how to get back. We can’t say more yet. We’re a small team that ships innovation, and here to prove our unique way of shaping the future of humans.
summary: Marsfinder is a navigation tool for astronauts walking or driving across Mars. Mars has no GPS, and a message to Earth takes over 11 minutes each way, so crews can't count on mission control to tell them where they are. We built two screens that stay in sync: a phone-sized heads-up display for the astronaut in the field, and a laptop view for planners on Earth. Planners draw a safe route around steep slopes and loose sand, and the astronaut follows it turn by turn, with oxygen and battery shown for every leg. Everything that crosses between the two screens arrives with the real Earth–Mars signal delay. To find their position, the astronaut takes a photo of the horizon. Our engine compares the skyline in the photo with horizons we computed from NASA elevation data and answers with a position, a heading and an honest uncertainty circle. We set it in Jezero Crater, where Perseverance landed, because the rover's photos let us test against real Mars images. Safety comes first: the app tells the crew when it isn't sure.
details:
What it does

Marsfinder helps a crew answer three questions during a surface walk: where am I, where should I go, and do I have enough oxygen to get there and back.

- Control (Earth): planners pick a target, and an A* route planner finds a path that avoids steep slopes and sand. They can see how much oxygen or battery each route will use, with a 20% reserve kept back. Anything they send reaches the field 11 min 20 s later, the real one-way delay.

- Field (astronaut): a phone-sized display. The map turns with the astronaut's heading, gives turn-by-turn directions, shows oxygen left and warns before the reserve runs low.

- Locate: the astronaut photographs the horizon. We trace the skyline in the photo, then compare it with horizon profiles we rendered in advance from about 22,800 points across the crater. The result is a position, which way the camera faces, and a 95% circle that shows how sure the engine is.

- Jezero map: an interactive map that zooms from the whole planet down to the Perseverance landing site, with slope and sand layers.

Data we used

NASA/JPL Mars Trek imagery and elevation: Viking MDIM 2.1, MRO CTX and HiRISE images, the CTX Jezero elevation model, and MOLA-HRSC elevation for the far terrain. The sand map is from USGS (Sun & Stack 2020, SIM 3464). For testing we used real Perseverance Navcam photos whose positions are known.

How we built it

The website uses Next.js, React and TypeScript, with OpenLayers and Leaflet for the maps and Vitest for tests. It builds to a static site, so it can run without a server. The positioning engine is written in Python (NumPy, rasterio, FastAPI). The horizon renderer agrees with a brute-force check to within a few thousandths of a degree, and it accounts for the curvature of Mars.

What we learned and how we tested it

We tested the engine on 300 simulated photos and 24 real rover positions. In simulation, when the engine says it is confident, 91% of answers are within 300 m. Real photos are harder. Nearby rocks and rover hardware confuse the skyline tracing, and fixing that is our next step. We decided early that the app must never claim to be sure when it isn't, so it shows its uncertainty instead of just a dot.

Why it matters and what's creative about it

Matching skylines is how people found their way before GPS, and it works anywhere we have elevation maps: Mars, the Moon, or a dead zone on Earth. Building the signal delay into the app makes planners and crew practise working the way they really will, with Earth always 11 minutes behind.

What we considered

- Astronaut safety first: oxygen reserves, slope and sand hazards, and clear warnings

- Bulky gloves: big buttons and only a few at a time

- Losing contact with Earth: the field screen keeps working on its own

- Honest uncertainty: the app shows how sure it is
